comparison: Both evaluate association detection claims (C1, C22-C29). OpenEval finds the statistical comparisons and honest reporting of limitations SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY about association quality compared to conventional methods, requesting additional validation of power, false positives, and false negatives despite the reported statistics.

Both evaluate cross-ancestry prediction claims (C4, C85-C88). Both find these claims SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the improvements complement rather than replace SNP-based approaches. Peer reviewers acknowledge the method 'can slightly improve polygenic scores' and increases portability across populations without specific critique.

Both evaluate fine-mapping performance claims (C2, C30-C33, C35, C42-C46, C100-C102). OpenEval finds comprehensive validation SUPPORTED across multiple approaches. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, raising critical concerns about false negatives from missing coding/splicing variants not modeled by Sei, and false positives from correlated neighboring windows, despite acknowledging the validation analyses.

Both evaluate pathway enrichment claims (C3, C50-C65). OpenEval finds extensive pathway results with significant p-values SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also find these SUPPORTED, explicitly stating 'the findings are largely biologically interpretable' and that HFS-based associations 'identify relevant causal pathways and genes.'

OpenEval evaluates functional enrichment patterns (C36-C41) as SUPPORTED with biologically meaningful results. Peer result R2 addresses overlapping fine-mapping concerns but expresses UNCERTAINTY due to methodological limitations including missing variant types and window correlation effects.

OpenEval evaluates tissue/cell type enrichment (C66-C73) as SUPPORTED with strong biological coherence. Peer result R3 addresses broader biological interpretability including these claims, finding them SUPPORTED as 'largely biologically interpretable.'

Both evaluate specific gene identification examples (C74-C80). OpenEval finds the RBBP5 case study SUPPORTED despite noting lack of independent experimental validation. Peer reviewers also find these SUPPORTED, noting that 'finemapping and pathway identification analyses suggest that HFS-based associations identify relevant causal pathways and genes.'

Both evaluate MHC region analysis (C81-C84). OpenEval finds the approach SUPPORTED but notes caution warranted due to MHC complexity and lack of independent validation. Peer reviewers also find these gene identification results SUPPORTED without specific challenge.

Both evaluate genome segmentation methodology (C13-C17). OpenEval finds the 4096 bp window strategy and LD characteristics SUPPORTED with well-documented quantitative results. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, questioning whether variants not in the center of 4kb regions are captured and how window choice affects results.

OpenEval evaluates comprehensive genome segmentation claims (C13-C20, C110) as SUPPORTED. Peer result R6 addresses subset of LD claims (C18-C20, C89) with UNCERTAINTY, raising concerns about window effects, variant capture outside window centers, and false positives from correlated neighboring windows.

Both evaluate low LD advantages (C89). OpenEval finds empirical support but rates extensibility to WGS as UNCERTAIN due to lack of demonstration. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY about the claimed LD advantages, questioning window effects and potential false positives from neighboring window correlations.

Both evaluate HFS limitations regarding incomplete variance capture (C94-C95). OpenEval finds the honest assessment SUPPORTED with ~70% variance capture consistent with prediction results. Peer reviewers also find these limitations SUPPORTED, accepting them as inherent constraints of the method.

Both evaluate limitations in coding regions (C105-C107). OpenEval finds the honest reporting and recommendation to prioritize SNP-based analysis in coding regions SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also find these SUPPORTED, explicitly noting HFS will 'miss coding variation as well as noncoding regulatory variants' not modeled by Sei.

Both evaluate computational requirements (C92-C93). OpenEval finds the transparent reporting of substantial computational costs SUPPORTED as important practical limitations. Peer reviewers also find these SUPPORTED, noting 'the proposed method is computationally intensive' without treating it as a critical flaw.

OpenEval evaluates robustness testing including sliding-window and indel analyses (C47-C49) as SUPPORTED, showing moderate consistency and appropriate characterization of limitations. Peer result R2 expresses broader UNCERTAINTY about fine-mapping methodology including concerns about window choice effects that relate to these robustness claims.

OpenEval evaluates simulation justifying reference sequence scores (C21) as SUPPORTED with 70% capture rate. Peer result R9 expresses UNCERTAINTY about the genome segmentation strategy including concerns about whether variants outside window centers are captured, which relates to this simulation's assumptions.
